🫱  7. Visitors Become Shadows or Kin
Outsiders are not distrusted by default—but they are observed carefully. A visitor who listens, respects tradition, 
and proves their value may be invited into the circle as a “bone-guest”, and over time, as kin-of-trust.
Some Flocks adopt outsiders permanently. Others allow them to walk beside rather than within, like moons near 
the spiral.
“Blood does not define kin. Memory and movement do.”
🧬  Life Within the Flock Means…
•You are never truly alone.
•Your failures are carried, and your triumphs are shared.
•You belong to something greater than yourself—not because of force, but because of choice, rhythm, and 
memory.
•Even across the multiverse, the Flock echoes in how you eat, how you protect others, and what you whisper 
to the stars when no one else can hear.

title_candidate: endurance, and battle prowess. Some orc tribes venerate their ancestors, especially those who played
text:
Orcs often worship deities or spirits that embody war, strength, endurance, and freedom. Many orcs 
see life as a test to prove their worth to these deities, with rituals that include feats of strength, 
endurance, and battle prowess. Some orc tribes venerate their ancestors, especially those who played 
a role in the rebellion against the Goblin empire, honoring them through songs, rites, and by invoking 
their spirits in times of need. Respect for the harsh realities of nature is also common, with orcs viewing 
themselves as one part of a larger struggle for survival.
While these traits and beliefs are common among orcs, individual orcs can vary widely, particularly in 
multiversal communities where diverse influences shape their identities. This diversity offers rich 
opportunities for orc characters to defy expectations and develop unique perspectives within the 
multiverse.

control. Abilities in this system are organized into tiers, and players must navigate branching choices to 
determine their Berserker's path. Every ability taken in the Berserker tree increases the difficulty of 
managing rage.
Core Mechanic: Rage Points
•Rage Points (RPs): Rage Points fuel the Berserker's abilities. Each ability costs a specific number of 
RPs to activate.
•Gaining RPs:
◦ Take damage: Gain 1 RP.
◦ Deal a critical hit: Gain 1 RP.
◦ An ally is reduced to 0 HP: Gain 2 RPs.
◦ Kill an enemy: Gain 2 RPs.
•Maximum RPs: Equal to 5 + your Constitution modifier.
•Uncontrolled Rage: If your RPs exceed your maximum, you must succeed on a Wisdom saving throw 
(DC = 10 + half your current RPs) or enter Uncontrolled Rage:
◦ Attack the nearest creature (ally or enemy).
◦ Lose the ability to take tactical actions or bonus actions until your RPs are reduced.
•Spending RPs: Abilities and moves require RPs to activate. Once spent, RPs are reduced, helping you 
avoid Uncontrolled Rage.

multiverse. Here are possible methods:

- Process:

causing it to implode.  
- Requirements:

  - Technology check (DC 14) to ensure the energy flow is properly directed.  
- Consequences:

  - Shadows attack in overwhelming waves during the ritual.  
  - The church may partially collapse, forcing the players to escape.

epicenter.  
- Requirements:

Core Actions
- Navigate Hazards: Roll D20 + Maneuverability modifier against a GM-defined DC.
  - Success: Progress without penalties.
  - Failure: Suffer consequences such as reduced Speed, Durability damage, or delays.
- Perform Stunts: Attempt sharp turns, jumps, or skids with the same mechanics.
- Use Modules or Equipment: Activate tools like smoke screens, oil slicks, or mounted weapons.
- Interact with Terrain: Clear debris, scout for shortcuts, or leverage environmental features.
---
Scenario-Specific Rules
1. High-Speed Chases
High-speed chases test driving skill and strategic thinking. Players may pursue or evade opponents.
Core Mechanics
- Distance Tracking: Track the distance between pursuers and evaders in feet. Chases start with an 
initial gap (e.g., 60–120 feet).
  - Evaders Escape: When the distance exceeds 300 feet.
  - Pursuers Catch: When the gap closes to 0 feet.
- Chase Actions:
  - Evasive Maneuvers (Evader): Roll D20 + Maneuverability modifier vs. pursuerʼs contested roll to 
increase distance by +20 feet on success.
  - Aggressive Driving (Pursuer): Roll contested checks to close the gap by -20 feet.
  - Boosting: Increase Speed by +10 feet, but roll D20 + Power (DC 15) or take 1d8 Durability damage.
Dynamic Hazards
- Introduce environmental elements such as:
  - Traffic/Obstacles: Maneuverability DC 15–20.
  - Weather Effects: Increase DCs by +5.

Combat Actions
- Attack: Ram or use improvised/mounted weapons.
  - Ramming: Roll D20 + Maneuverability modifier vs. targetʼs contested roll. Deal Speed/10 + 1d8 (small 
vehicle) or higher damage for larger vehicles. Both vehicles take damage.
  - Weapons: Mounted weapons follow standard attack rolls (e.g., D20 + Dexterity modifier + Weapon 
modifier).
- Defensive Maneuvers: Roll D20 + Maneuverability modifier to evade attacks. Success imposes 
disadvantage on the attacker.
- Deployables: Use tools like smoke screens, oil slicks, or reinforced panels for tactical advantages.
Special Combat Scenarios
- Demolition Derbies: Last vehicle standing wins; prioritize ramming and durability.
- Arena Deathmatches: Combine hazards, power-ups (e.g., repair kits), and objectives for dynamic 
combat.
---
4. Urban Exploration
Navigating complex environments emphasizes creativity and teamwork.
Recon and Surveillance
- Blend into surroundings or tail targets:
  - Roll Stealth or Deception (DC 15) to avoid detection.
  - Roll Perception or Investigation to gather intel or maintain line of sight.
- Dynamic Challenges: Handle moving targets, changing terrain, or NPC interference with appropriate 
skill checks.
Search and Rescue
- Reach and extract NPCs from hazardous areas:
  - Navigate terrain as above, then:
    - Find Targets: Perception (DC 15).
    - Rescue Actions: Clear debris (Strength/Engineering DC 15–20), stabilize injured NPCs (Medicine DC 
10–20).

Seafaring vehicles
4. Seafaring Vehicles
a. Operation and Navigation
Seafaring vehicles are designed for operation on water, including oceans, seas, rivers, and lakes. 
Navigating these vehicles requires specific skills to handle different water conditions and to manage 
marine environments effectively.
- Starting and Stopping: No check required under normal conditions.
- Basic Navigation: Roll a d20 + Seafaring Vehicles skill modifier against DC 10.
- Advanced Navigation: For navigating through challenging areas like reefs or crowded ports, roll a d20 
+ Seafaring Vehicles skill modifier against DC 15.
- Emergency Maneuvers: For sudden changes in direction or avoiding obstacles, roll a d20 + Seafaring 
Vehicles skill modifier against DC 20.
b. Water Conditions and Challenges
Navigating seafaring vehicles involves dealing with various water conditions and challenges that can 
affect the vehicleʼs performance.
- Calm Waters: No additional modifiers.
- Rough Waters: Add +2 to the DC for all navigation checks.
- Stormy Seas: Add +5 to the DC for all navigation checks.
- Foggy Conditions: Add +3 to the DC for all navigation checks.
- Ice and Cold Waters: Add +4 to the DC for all navigation checks and require an Engineering skill check 
(DC 15) to ensure the vehicleʼs systems are not affected by the cold.
d. Combat and Defense
Seafaring vehicles can engage in combat and require defensive capabilities to protect against threats. 
Combat involves both offensive and defensive maneuvers, as well as the use of onboard weaponry.
- Combat Maneuvers: Roll a d20 + Seafaring Vehicles skill modifier against the opponentʼs roll (d20 + 
Seafaring Vehicles skill modifier). Higher roll succeeds.
  - Ramming: Opposed roll against the targetʼs maneuvering check. If successful, target takes damage.
  - Evasive Actions: Opposed roll against the attackerʼs targeting roll. If successful, the vehicle evades 
the attack.

Swamps: A Quagmire of Survival and Secrets
Overview
Swamps are waterlogged lowlands, thick with vegetation, mud, and decay. They can appear as tranquil 
wetlands or ominous, fog-laden expanses. Swamps often harbor hidden dangers beneath deceptively 
still waters, including wildlife, diseases, and supernatural forces. This section outlines how to handle 
gameplay in these environments, including movement rules, hazards, and key encounters.
Environmental Features
1.Terrain Types:
•Shallow Water: Difficult terrain, slowing movement to half speed.
•Deep Water: Requires swimming; Strength (Athletics) checks to avoid exhaustion after long 
periods.
•Mud Flats: Heavy mud acts as difficult terrain. Failed Dexterity saving throws may cause 
characters to sink (DC 12 to avoid becoming restrained).

1.Weak Structures:
•Some parts of the city are dangerously unstable. Loud noises or sudden impacts can trigger 
collapses, forcing characters to make Dexterity saving throws (DC 14) to avoid 3d6 bludgeoning 
damage.
2.Ancient Curses:
•The ruins may be protected by forgotten magic. Triggering these defenses requires a Wisdom 
saving throw (DC 15) to resist. A failed save could result in:
◦ Lingering Curse: Characters cannot leave the ruins until the curse is dispelled.
◦ Crushing Weight: Gravity increases around the target, halving movement speed until the 
curse is lifted.
3.Electric Eels or Jellyfish:
•Characters swimming through certain areas may encounter creatures that deliver electric 
shocks. A failed Dexterity saving throw (DC 13) results in 2d8 lightning damage and 
disadvantage on all movement-related rolls for 1 minute.
4.Magical Wards:
•Runes etched into the walls may detect intruders, releasing energy blasts or calling guardians. 
Wisdom (Arcana) checks (DC 14) allow players to spot and disarm these wards.
Flora and Fauna
1.Hostile Creatures:
•Sharks or Deep-Sea Predators: Fast-moving predators that patrol the ruins. They are attracted 
to movement and blood in the water.
•Merrow or Sirens: Aquatic creatures that ambush adventurers and lure them into traps.
•Aquatic Undead: The spirits of those who perished in the sunken city, now cursed to guard its 
secrets.
•Kraken Spawn: Small, aggressive offspring of a kraken, eager to devour anything that enters 
their domain.
2.Helpful Creatures:
•Dolphins: Curious and friendly, dolphins may guide the players toward air pockets or safer paths.
•Sea Turtles: Slow but wise, these creatures may carry information about the ruins or provide 
transport through currents.
3.Useful Plants:
•Glowkelp: Provides bioluminescence and can be used to light underwater paths.
•Coral Pods: Contain healing properties. When consumed, they restore 1d8 HP.
•Pearlweed: Can be harvested to create potions that allow water-breathing for 1 hour.

   - Mechanics:

Movement and Navigation Rules
1.Movement in Zero Gravity:
•Characters can propel themselves in a direction by pushing off an object, moving 30 feet per 
push. Without something to grab onto, they drift in the same direction until stopped.
•Maneuvering with a propulsion device (e.g., thruster pack) requires Dexterity (Acrobatics) 
checks (DC 13) to avoid spinning out of control.
2.Tethering and Anchoring:
•Tethers are essential to prevent drifting away in the void. Tethered movement allows characters 
to maintain control, while untethered movement requires Dexterity checks (DC 14) to change 
direction or stop.
•Using magnetic boots or grappling hooks to secure a position prevents drift and can stabilize 
movement on larger structures, like space debris or derelict ships.
3.Orientation and Navigation:
•Without landmarks, characters must succeed on Wisdom (Survival) checks (DC 15) to maintain 
orientation. Failure means they become disoriented, potentially drifting off course or struggling 
to find their bearings.
Void Hazards
1.Radiation Exposure:
Space is filled with cosmic radiation. Each hour in open space, characters without radiation 
protection must make a Constitution saving throw (DC 14) or suffer 1 level of exhaustion from 
radiation sickness.
2.Micrometeor Impacts:
Tiny, high-velocity particles travel through space, posing a constant risk. Roll a d20 every hour in 
the void; on a 1, characters must make Dexterity saving throws (DC 15) to avoid 1d10 piercing 
damage from micrometeor impacts.
3.Extreme Cold and Heat:
Open space alternates between extreme cold and intense sunlight. Characters without thermal 
shielding experience temperature fluctuations that require Constitution saving throws (DC 13) 
every 10 minutes to avoid 1d6 cold or radiant damage.
4.Oxygen Supply Limitations:
Space suits have limited oxygen supplies, usually enough for 8 hours. For each hour without a 
refill, characters must track their oxygen use carefully. Once oxygen is depleted, characters begin 
to suffocate.

Encounters and Challenges
1.Asteroid Miners and Rival Prospectors:
Mining vessels and prospectors search the asteroid field for resources, often competing over 
claims. Characters may encounter friendly miners, hostile rivals, or territorial prospectors who 
demand a cut of any found resources.
2.Space Pirates and Scavengers:
Pirates and scavengers use asteroid fields as cover, waiting to ambush unsuspecting ships. These 
hostile forces may try to disable ships or loot any valuable materials.
3.Lost Wreckage and Abandoned Outposts:
Old mining stations, wrecked ships, or abandoned outposts drift among the asteroids, potentially 
holding valuable equipment or resources, but also risks such as collapsed structures or rogue 
security systems.
4.Radiation Pockets and Ion Storms:
Radiation pockets or passing ion storms can interfere with sensors and navigation. Ships or 
individuals passing through must make Constitution saving throws (DC 15) to avoid exhaustion or 
system malfunctions.
5.Asteroid Worms and Rock-Dwelling Predators:
Some large asteroids may harbor alien creatures adapted to the vacuum. These predators ambush 
intruders, requiring characters to make Dexterity saving throws (DC 14) to avoid surprise attacks or 
take 2d6 piercing damage.
Resting in an Asteroid Field
•Short Rest:
Short rests can only be taken in safe, sheltered spots like inside a mining ship or behind a large 
asteroid. Roll a d20; on a 5 or lower, a nearby hazard (e.g., drifting asteroid or micrometeor) 
interrupts the rest.

The dense clouds of the nebula can hide derelict ships, abandoned research stations, or 
temporary outposts. Characters may come across wrecks or structures containing useful 
resources, but these areas often have failing life support or residual radiation.
2.Nebula-Dwelling Entities:
Strange lifeforms adapted to the nebula environment may dwell within the clouds. These entities 
might be curious or territorial, attacking if threatened. Characters must make Charisma (Animal 
Handling or Persuasion) checks (DC 15) to calm or communicate with them.
3.Ghostly Transmissions and Distorted Signals:
Ghostly echoes of lost transmissions play through the nebula, confusing navigators. Attempting to 
decode these signals requires Intelligence (Investigation) checks (DC 14) to separate real 
communications from ghostly echoes, potentially leading to lost relics or expeditions.
4.Resource Deposits in Dangerous Zones:
Rich deposits of plasma crystals, ionized gases, or rare elements may be found but often lie within 
high-radiation or energy-anomalous areas. Characters scavenging in these zones must make 
Constitution saving throws (DC 15) every 10 minutes to avoid exhaustion or radiation poisoning.
5.Pirates and Scavengers in Nebula Cover:
Pirates and scavengers use the nebula as cover to ambush passing ships or explore hidden 
resources. Characters must make Dexterity saving throws (DC 15) to avoid surprise attacks, or 
Charisma (Intimidation) checks (DC 14) to negotiate safe passage.

❌  Toon Vulnerabilities
Toons are powerful, flexible, and nearly indestructible under the right conditions—but they are not invincible. 
Their connection to toon physics leaves them vulnerable when faced with logic, disbelief, and reality 
enforcement. These vulnerabilities allow GMs and players to meaningfully interact with toons in structured or 
cross-genre campaigns.
🧱  1. Reality Anchors
Toons lose functionality when exposed to intense logical or realistic environments. These may include:
•Anti-Toon Fields: Zones or devices that suppress toon abilities and gag logic.
•Grade 0 Realities: Worlds with strictly enforced physics, causality, and continuity.
•Serious Narrative Tone: Genres such as hard sci-fi, horror, or tragedy may naturally weaken toon logic.
Effects While Anchored:
•Cannot use Stretch & Squash or subtype-specific narrative effects.
•Lose access to Toon Save.
•Take double damage from logic-based weapons, tools, or attacks specifically designed to counter unreality.
•Instabilities may become suppressed, glitchy, or unpredictable.
🧠  2. Disbelief Collapse
Toons rely on a mix of internal conviction and audience buy-in. If they are not perceived as “funny,” “fitting,” or 
“entertaining,” their powers can weaken or fail.
Disbelief Collapse Triggers:
•Playing to a crowd that rejects or ignores them.
•Violating genre tone or narrative coherence.
•Repeating a joke that has already failed.
Effects:
•Roll a Disbelief Save (DC 10 + number of observers). On a failure:
◦ Toon powers glitch or fizzle.

If a toonʼs subtype warps the rules (e.g., Fourth-Waller or Narrative Virus), allow it—but warn the table first or 
restrict it to set encounters.
🧠  Design Tip: Let the tone be silly, but keep the logic structured.
📉  3. Use Vulnerabilities to Create Stakes
Despite their cartoon absurdity, toons can be weakened. Use reality anchors, disbelief collapse, or genre clash
as tools:
•In serious scenes, toon powers might glitch or misfire.
•Logic-heavy PCs (like detectives, scientists, or clerics) may "stabilize" reality near them.
•Villains may use anti-toon tech to suppress toon heroes.
These vulnerabilities let players interact with toons as solvable problems, not untouchable chaos engines.
🌀  4. Control Spread of Toon Physics
Unless youʼre running a full Unreal Zone arc, be cautious about how far toon logic spreads.
Toons can destabilize:
•Entire encounters
•Local NPCs
•Environmental physics
•Player expectations
Limit the area of effect (e.g., "within 30 ft," "for 1 minute") or require scene ownership ("only when the toon is 
the sceneʼs focus").
If toon logic becomes infectious (Narrative Virus subtype), clearly telegraph consequences, and allow PCs a way 
to isolate or resist it.
🎙  5. Use Behavioral Tags for Roleplay Hooks
Tags like Brickwaller, Sadistic, or Audience-Seeking shape the personality of a toon. These help:
•Define the toonʼs threat level.
•Set up non-combat complications (e.g., a Brickwaller surgeon “treating” a healthy PC).
•Determine if a toon requires containment or supervision.
🎲  Optional Mechanic: NPCs with 2+ high-risk tags may require a “Toon Containment Check” at the start of 
chaotic scenes.

8. Timeline Reality Tunneling
“Itʼs not about where youʼre going. Itʼs about reaching the version of events where you already arrived.”

8.1 What Is Tunneling?
Timeline Reality Tunneling is the process of creating a metaphysical shortcut—a direct tunnel through the 
multiversal structure—linking one version of reality to another. This bypasses traditional methods of travel and 
anchors, allowing the character to leap to a timeline or parallel version that diverged from a key moment.

timeline or version that may not yet exist, should not exist, or has been collapsed.

A shaman may spend 1 hour in meditation with their totem to:

⚖  Roleplay Notes: Totem-Based Taboos
Each totem may impose soft roleplay restrictions known as taboos—behaviors that offend the spiritʼs 
nature. While not enforced mechanically, breaking a taboo may:
•Strain or sever the totem bond
•Invoke minor curses or spiritual disfavor
•Require an atonement ritual
Examples:
•Wolf: Betraying allies or abandoning companions in danger
•Crow: Withholding important knowledge
•Deer: Wanton destruction of life or nature
These enrich the shamanʼs narrative and moral landscape.
🔮  Optional: Totem Duality or Evolution
At higher tiers (Tier 5+), some GMs may allow the shaman to:
•Evolve their totem (e.g., from Wolf →  Dire Wolf or Moon Wolf)
•Gain a secondary totem, representing growth or transformation
•Form a unique fusion totem based on the playerʼs journey
This option should be tied to significant story arcs and approved by the GM.
🌿  Spirit Animals
Spirit animals are temporary, situational allies that respond to the shamanʼs state of mind, environment, or 
spiritual request. Unlike the lifelong bond of a totem animal, spirit animals represent fluid, dynamic 
connections to the spirit world, manifesting to grant short-term powers, insight, or assistance.
Where the totem animal defines the shamanʼs core nature, spirit animals reflect their present need.

title_candidate: The Kola-Ha: Background Options for Multiversal
text:
The Kola-Ha: Background Options for Multiversal
The Kola-Ha are a species of amphibious beings deeply attuned to the oceanʼs rhythms, masters of bio-
magical engineering, and keepers of ancient wisdom. Their underwater societies thrive in harmony with 
nature, crafting living architecture, organic artifacts, and symbiotic technology.  
---
Homeworld Types  
Each Kola-Ha originates from a unique aquatic environment, shaping their physical adaptations, 
knowledge, and worldview.  
1. The Shoals (Ancient coral cities infused with bio-magical lifeforms.)  
- Core Benefits: +2 Arcana or Nature, +1 Engineering, proficiency in Bio-Magic & Living Architecture.  
- XP Options:  
  - Architect of the Depths (400 XP): Once per session, detect structural weaknesses or strengths in 
organic or magical buildings.  
  - Coral Communion (600 XP): Gain the ability to communicate with coral-based creatures and 
structures.  
2. The Abyssal Trench (The lightless depths where only the strongest endure.)  
- Core Benefits: +2 Survival or Athletics, +1 Stealth, proficiency in Cold Resistance & Deep Sea 
Hunting.  
- XP Options:  
  - Abyssal Predator (400 XP): Gain advantage on Dexterity (Stealth) in darkness.  
  - Pressure Adaptation (600 XP): Reduce cold and pressure-based damage by half.  
3. The Bioluminescent Reefs (A vibrant underwater expanse of glowing marine life.)  
- Core Benefits: +2 Perception or Medicine, +1 Animal Handling, proficiency in Bioluminescent Life & 
Medicinal Coral.  
- XP Options:  
  - Glow of the Depths (400 XP): Emit bioluminescent light in a 15-ft radius at will.  
  - Healing Coral (600 XP): Once per long rest, use bio-magical coral to heal 2d6 HP.
